title: The parrot drops
hookLine: hearing the caged parrot's words, a wild parrot falls as if dead, and the merchant reports it home (Masnavi 1)

lines: A HARMLESS TEXT LANDS LIKE A STONE.
cards: You send a text you think is harmless. A joke, a bit of news, a passing comment. Then the little dots appear, and disappear, and appear again, and you realize, too late, that your words landed like a stone.
Words can do things no one meant them to do. The merchant arrives in India. He finds the forests, and the parrots flashing green in the trees.
And, faithful to his promise, he delivers his parrot's message. Today, the parrot drops.

teach.b: He stands under the trees and repeats his parrot's words exactly: a parrot who loves you is shut in a cage in my house; is it right that it wastes away while you fly free?

teach.h: A WILD PARROT FALLS, AS IF DEAD.
teach.b: As soon as he's finished, one of the wild parrots begins to tremble. It shakes, loses its grip, and falls from the branch to the ground. Still.
As if dead. The merchant is horrified. What have I done?
I've killed a creature with a sentence. Maybe this bird and mine were kin, as close as body and soul. Why did I ever carry that message?

teach.h: WORDS ARE FIRE, AN ARROW SHOT.
teach.b: Words, he says, are like flint and steel: what springs from the tongue is fire. Once spoken, they're an arrow already shot; you can't call them back.
They travel, and they do things in the world, often things you didn't intend. So guard your tongue. But there's another side.

teach.h: AND MY GIFT? WHAT DID YOU SAY?
teach.b: Those words did something no gift could have done. They moved a wild bird so deeply it fell from the tree, because words reach inside. The merchant finishes his trading, sad, and goes home.
He hands out the gifts. Then the parrot in its cage says: and my gift? What did you see?
What did you say? The merchant doesn't want to answer. He's ashamed, and he knows the story will hurt.
But he tells it. What those words do next is tomorrow's story.
For today: every message does something.

how: Teachers of the Masnavi often pause at this scene to discuss Rumi's reflections on speech, that words spoken cannot be taken back, before continuing the parrot's story.

o: a spoken word that can't be called back
a sign pointing the way you should go
a sharp insult aimed to hurt someone

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: trembles and falls, as if dead

s: the merchant forgets to deliver the greeting
he delivers it word for word, and a wild parrot falls from the tree.
Rumi compares spoken words to an arrow already shot
once spoken, they can't be called back; they travel and act in the world.
the merchant is glad to tell his parrot what happened
he's ashamed and doesn't want to answer, but he tells it.

games.q: you're the merchant, home again. your parrot asks what happened in India. you know the story will hurt. what do you do?
o: tell it the truth, though you're ashamed.
change the subject to the other gifts.
games.why: he tells the truth. and what those words do next is tomorrow's story.

practice: Think back to a message that changed your day: good news, bad news, a single sentence from someone. Where were you, and what happened in your body when you heard it?
Then recall one you sent that did more than you expected, for good or for ill, and just notice the power running both ways.

wordCard.voice: Arrow. Rumi's image for a spoken word: once loosed, like an arrow already shot, it can't be called back. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian: a message, word sent by someone. the only gift the parrot asked for.
